lines: Thermal-Aware Scheduling for Edge Inference
Authors: Ines Duarte and Kofi Asante (fictional authors; synthetic evaluation paper).
Identifier: doi:10.5555/ras-eval.p07 (fictional, not registered).
Abstract
We schedule neural network inference on edge devices using on-chip temperature forecasts.
The scheduler cuts p95 latency by 23% and thermal throttling events from 41 to 9 per hour.
Introduction
Edge devices lower their clock speed when the chip gets too hot, so latency becomes erratic.
Reactive governors respond only after throttling has started and cannot plan ahead.
Inference workloads are often bursty, which makes short-term temperature spikes common.
A scheduler that predicts temperature can delay low-priority jobs before throttling begins.
Such planning must stay cheap, because the forecaster runs on the same constrained device.
We therefore restrict the forecaster to a linear model that needs no accelerator support.
The goal is predictable latency for interactive requests rather than maximum throughput.
We compare against first-come-first-served scheduling with the default thermal governor.
Our contribution is a scheduler that uses forecasts, together with measurements on devices.
Methods
The forecaster is a linear model over the last 20 temperature readings sampled at 10 Hz.
Jobs are deferred when the forecast exceeds 78 degrees Celsius within the next two seconds.
Deferred jobs wait in a priority queue and are resumed once the forecast falls again.
Interactive requests are never deferred for longer than 300 milliseconds in this design.
We evaluated three device types: a phone SoC, a single-board computer and a drone controller.
Each device ran the same image classification model with a batch size of one request.
Every experiment lasted two hours at an ambient temperature of 24 degrees Celsius.
Latency was logged per request, and throttling events were read from the kernel log.
Results
Across the three devices, p95 latency fell by 23% relative to first-come-first-served.
Throttling events dropped from 41 to 9 per hour on average across the three devices.
Energy per inference rose by 4% because deferred jobs later ran at higher clock speeds.
The phone SoC showed the largest latency gain, a 31% reduction of p95 latency.
The single-board computer improved by 27%, with most gains during long bursts.
Median latency changed by less than 2% on every device, so the gain lies in the tail.
Forecast error stayed below 1.5 degrees Celsius for 95% of the prediction windows.
The scheduler itself used less than 1% of processor time on each of the devices.
Discussion
The drone controller benefited least, with a 9% latency reduction.
Its cooling was already adequate, so the chip rarely approached the threshold.
Longer forecast horizons made the scheduler defer too many jobs in our trials.
A threshold below 78 degrees Celsius reduced throttling further but hurt throughput.
Results may differ for workloads with large batches or for devices with active fans.
We did not study multi-tenant settings where several models share one device.
Integrating the forecaster into the kernel governor is left for future work.
The measurements cover a single ambient temperature, which limits generality.
Conclusion
Forecast-driven deferral keeps tail latency predictable on thermally limited devices.
The approach needs only a small linear model and a priority queue per device.
References
[1] P. Laine. Dynamic Thermal Management for Mobile Processors. 2023.
[2] G. Ortiz. Tail Latency on Embedded Inference Hardware. 2024.
Low-Light Wildlife Detection with Event Cameras
Authors: Joon Park and Emma Laurent (fictional authors; synthetic evaluation paper).
Identifier: doi:10.5555/ras-eval.p08 (fictional, not registered).
Abstract
We detect nocturnal animals with an event camera and a spiking neural detector.
At 2 lux the detector reaches a mean recall of 0.71 across nine species.
Introduction
Camera traps at night rely on infrared illumination, which can disturb some animals.
Event cameras report brightness changes per pixel and work at very low light levels.
Their sparse output suits spiking detectors that run on low-power hardware in the field.
Few studies measure how detection quality changes as the scene gets darker.
We collect clips in forests and report recall at several controlled light levels.
Our aim is to find the light level below which detection becomes unreliable.
We also compare the power draw of the event camera with an infrared reference camera.
The dataset and labels are described in the methods section of this paper.
Methods
Events are accumulated into 4 temporal bins of 25 milliseconds each.
The detector was trained on 14,200 labelled clips from 3 forest sites.
Clips were labelled by two ecologists who marked the species and a bounding box.
Light levels were measured with a calibrated lux meter placed next to the camera.
We report recall because false negatives matter most for population surveys.
Each site contributed clips from both summer and winter recording periods.
Training used a fixed learning schedule without any per-site tuning at all.
Test clips come from recording nights that were not used during training.
Results
Figure 3. Recall per species at 2 lux.
Figure 3 shows per-species recall; the exact values appear only in the figure.
Mean recall fell from 0.71 at 2 lux to 0.52 at 0.5 lux across all nine species.
False positives were most often caused by moving branches in windy conditions.
Recall was stable across the two recording seasons for most of the species.
Small animals such as mice were detected less often than larger mammals.
Detection latency on the field hardware stayed below 40 milliseconds per clip.
Adding a fifth temporal bin did not change mean recall in our ablation runs.
Clips with rain produced more events but did not reduce recall noticeably.
Discussion
The event camera consumed 0.9 W compared with 2.6 W for the infrared reference camera.
Lower power allows longer deployments on the same battery in remote locations.
Detection below 0.5 lux may need longer bins or a more sensitive sensor model.
Branch motion remains the main source of errors and needs better filtering.
Our sites were temperate forests, so other habitats may behave differently.
Species with little motion at night are hard to detect with events alone.
A combined event and infrared system could cover both situations in future.
Ethics approval covered passive recording only, without any animal handling.
Conclusion
Event cameras detect nocturnal wildlife reliably down to about 2 lux at low power.
Per-species values should be read from Figure 3 in the original file.
References
[1] M. Haddad. Spiking Detectors for Neuromorphic Vision. 2024.
[2] B. Keller. Camera Traps and Animal Disturbance. 2022.
Federated Learning for Hospital Readmission Prediction
Authors: Sara Haile and Luca Bianchi (fictional authors; synthetic evaluation paper).
Identifier: doi:10.5555/ras-eval.p09 (fictional, not registered).
Abstract
Seven hospitals trained a readmission model without sharing patient records.
The federated model reached an AUROC of 0.78, close to 0.79 for pooled training.
Introduction
Readmission within 30 days is costly for hospitals and harmful for patients.
Prediction models need data from many hospitals to generalise across populations.
Legal rules often prevent hospitals from pooling patient records in one place.
Federated learning trains a shared model while each hospital keeps its own data.
We test whether federated training can match a model trained on pooled records.
We also measure the cost of adding differential privacy to the shared updates.
Our cohort comes from seven hospitals of very different sizes in one region.
All analyses were approved by the ethics boards of the participating hospitals.
Methods
Each hospital ran 5 local epochs per round for 60 rounds of federated training.
Updates were clipped to norm 1.0 and aggregated with secure summation.
The model is a gradient-boosted ensemble distilled into a small neural network.
Features include diagnoses, length of stay, age group and prior admissions.
The outcome is an unplanned readmission within 30 days of hospital discharge.
Pooled training on the same features serves as an upper reference model.
Each hospital held out 20% of its admissions for the final evaluation step.
We repeated federated training with three random seeds for every setting.
Results
Per-hospital AUROC values are listed in Table 4, which is provided as a scanned image.
The smallest hospital, with 1,900 admissions, gained the most from federation.
Differential privacy with epsilon 8 reduced the federated AUROC to 0.75.
Calibration of the federated model was similar to that of the pooled model.
Training finished in 11 hours of wall-clock time across all seven hospitals.
Communication per round stayed below 4 megabytes for every participating site.
Hospitals with fewer than 5,000 admissions benefited more than large hospitals.
No hospital performed worse with the federated model than with a local model.
Discussion
Federated training nearly matched pooled training without moving patient records.
The privacy cost of epsilon 8 may be acceptable for decision support but not for all uses.
Small hospitals gain the most, which supports regional collaboration on such models.
Our cohort covers one region, so external validation in other regions is needed.
Scanned appendix tables should be converted to text before any automated reuse.
Future work will test personalisation layers for hospitals with unusual case mixes.
Secure summation added little overhead compared with the local training time.
Clinicians reviewed the top features and found them clinically plausible.
Conclusion
Federated learning offers near-pooled readmission prediction across seven hospitals.
Per-hospital values remain available only in the scanned Table 4 of the original.
References
[1] E. Novak. Secure Aggregation for Federated Health Models. 2024.
[2] D. Ferreira. Readmission Risk Scores Revisited. 2023.
